arduous

/AR-doo-us/ — stress on AR · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Something that is arduous takes a great deal of effort and is exhausting to get through.

Learning to play the violin is an arduous process that rewards daily patience.

Example

The mountaineers' arduous climb took four days of struggling through thin air, loose rock, and treacherous weather.

Ardu- (from Latin arduus, meaning steep or difficult) + -ous (full of, possessing the quality) = full of steepness, full of difficulty. Unlike anomalous and anonymous, the base ardu- is not a standalone English word—it's opaque. The -ous suffix tells you this is a 'full of' adjective, and Latin supplies the meaning: this climb feels like walking straight uphill. Takes the -uous spelling.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

grueling: Grueling means exhausting to the point of punishment — a grueling race grinds competitors down until finishing feels like survival. Arduous is heavy but not punishing: an arduous project demands long, steep, sustained effort and leaves you drained rather than battered. A grueling day beats you up; an arduous one wears you down.

strenuous: Strenuous means demanding great physical energy — strenuous exercise leaves muscles burning and lungs heaving. Arduous is wider: it covers any long, difficult effort, mental as much as physical, like an arduous translation or an arduous legal battle. Every strenuous hike is hard on the body; an arduous task may never raise your pulse.

laborious: Laborious describes work that is slow, heavy, and full of tedious steps — laboriously copying a long list by hand. It emphasizes the plodding effort itself. Arduous emphasizes the toll: a task so steep and demanding that it exhausts you. Filing a thousand pages is laborious; crossing a mountain range is arduous.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

easy: requiring little effort or skill

effortless: done smoothly with no strain at all

Where it sits · how much effort it drains from you

tiring → tough → demanding → arduous

tiring vs. arduous: A tiring chore wears you out a little, but an arduous one leaves you completely drained.

tough vs. arduous: A tough workout tests your strength; an arduous workout pushes you to your absolute limit.

demanding vs. arduous: A demanding project asks a lot of you, but an arduous project asks nearly everything you have.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — ardu: steep, high — from Latin arduus; never became a standalone English word (Latin (arduus))

Suffix — -ous: full of (Latin (-osus))

Put it together: The base ardu- is not an English word on its own; it comes from Latin arduus, 'steep.' Add -ous ('full of') and arduous means 'full of steepness' — a task that feels like climbing a steep hill, demanding effort every step of the way.

Use the root in a new word: arduously: The rescue team worked arduously through the night to clear the blocked mountain pass.

Word Building

Word Choice

neutral to formal

Reach for arduous to describe a long process, journey, or task that tests endurance and will—learning a language, climbing a mountain, writing a thesis. It carries a sense of uphill effort and the steep climb to completion. Arduous suggests not just hard, but persistently, exhaustingly hard.
